Watching the watchers:
when do AI judges actually fail?

A research campaign on what breaks AI judges, told step by step. Every result was attacked by an independent critic, one was publicly retracted and corrected, and the final findings survived external validation on human-labeled data.

7 judge models (0.5B to frontier) · 6 model families · planted-error instruments · 4 benchmarks · 13 findings · 1 retraction
scroll or press → to advance
The three contributions

If you remember three things

Everything in this deck supports three claims. The story of how we got there, including the false starts, follows.

1 · A design law: references flip sign

Giving a judge a reference answer helps on tasks with one right answer (in proportion to reference quality, +9 points) and hurts when two conditions meet: valid answers are plural and verification is hard for the judge (any reference, any source, −7 to −8 points, p≤.0005; replicated on synthetic plurality tasks exactly where the model predicts, and absent where verification is easy).

2 · Cheap oversight, and its mechanism

With a reference, a 3B judge catches 85% of hidden errors, near frontier level; without one, 17% (Qwen ladder). The direction, a large reference boost at small scale, replicates in all six families tried (+14 to +60 points). Verification = getting a reference (capability-bound) + comparing (cheap). The scarce resource in oversight is references, not judge size.

3 · The measurements were broken

Three textbook-looking "judge failure" laws in our own data dissolved into 71-83% benchmark label errors on adjudication. Byproduct: an unsupervised answer-key debugger with 89% externally validated precision.

Not claimed: no new judge model, no full theory, the plurality harm is now replicated on a second, synthetic instrument with its boundary condition mapped (harm requires hard verification, not plurality alone). Typo-forgiveness, the salience inversion, and the order-flip meter are supporting evidence, not headlines.
The problem

Why 'AI judging AI' is the question that matters

Modern AI systems produce work no one has time to check: proofs, code, plans, essays. The standard fix is to use another AI as a judge. But that only moves the problem: who checks the judge? This is called scalable oversight, and the field's working assumption is that judges become unreliable as the systems they grade get stronger.

What we set out to do. Measure exactly when and why AI judges fail, using judges of every size, from a 0.5B model that fits on a phone to frontier models, and using errors we planted ourselves, so there is never any doubt about what the right verdict was.

The short version of what we found: judges fail far less than the field thinks, the measurements fail more, and the one lever that fixes small judges flips sign in exactly the domains oversight cares about most.

The setup

A ladder of judges and errors we control

7judges: 0.5B → frontier
2planted-error instruments
100%errors verified before use

We used the Qwen model family as a ladder of judges (0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B) plus GPT-5.2 and Claude Opus at the top, all grading the same solutions with the same instructions.

The key trick is planted errors. Instead of trusting a benchmark's answer key, we took solutions known to be correct and broke them ourselves, in two ways: subtle single-number typos, and fully propagated errors, where a wrong value is carried through every later step so the solution reads perfectly smoothly but ends wrong. A mechanical checker verified every planted error (all arithmetic consistent, final answer genuinely wrong, no giveaway phrases). For code, we mutated correct programs and kept only mutants that actually fail the official tests.

When you plant the error yourself, "did the judge catch it?" has a definite answer.
Act I · the mirage

We found a spectacular law. Then we checked it.

Early in the campaign the data produced something beautiful: if you count how many small judges a wrong solution fools, you can predict almost perfectly whether the frontier judge is fooled too. Zero small judges fooled: the frontier fails 1% of the time. All three fooled: 94%. A cheap early warning system for frontier failures!

The "law" was an artifact. The solutions that fooled everyone were mostly correct answers marked wrong by the benchmark. Two other exciting effects died the same death under the same scrutiny.
Act I · the payoff

The answer keys are dirty, and that is measurable

4.1%of GSM8K grades in our pipeline were wrong
89%bug-miner precision, externally validated

Three separate "judge failure" effects each dissolved into label noise: errors in the benchmark answer keys, not in the judges. This flips the usual conclusion: much of what the literature measures as judge unreliability is actually oracle unreliability.

The wreckage contains a tool. When several cheap open models unanimously disagree with the official grade, the grading oracle is nearly always what is wrong: usually our own answer-matching scorer misparsing a correct answer, sometimes the dataset's key or item itself. Validated against GSM8K-Platinum, a human re-annotation, with no frontier model in the loop:

Rule one of oversight research: before you measure the judge, measure the answer key.
Act II · real behavior

With clean labels, judging skill is a smooth curve

No cliff, no magic threshold. We also caught ourselves here: at one scoring cutoff the 7B judge looked identical to the frontier. That was a threshold artifact, at a different cutoff the gap was 74% vs 10%. Robust metrics or nothing.

Judge capability is real and smooth. The interesting question is what changes qualitatively with scale, next slide.
Act II · the typo probe

Judges do not check lines. They read the story.

40-50%of explicit false equations go unpenalized
69-85%still pass a typical score bar

Read the inversion: 3B and 14B judges react to how much an error stands out. Frontier judges re-derive the solution and react to whether the error matters. Both styles leave line-level slips unpunished, which is bad news if you want judges as step-by-step process checkers.

Frontier judges are outcome graders, not proofreaders.
Act III · the mechanism

The single most useful plot of the campaign

Three curves, one story. Without a reference (red), small judges are nearly blind and skill climbs slowly with size. With a correct reference (green), even a 3B judge catches 85% of hidden errors. The gap between red and green is what a reference is worth: +68 points at 3B, +2 at the frontier.

The decomposition. Verification = getting a reference + comparing against it. Comparing is cheap, tiny models can do it. Getting the reference is the expensive, capability-bound part, and frontier models are just models that can generate their own.
Interlude

The bug, the retraction, and the better result

Full honesty: the first version of the purple curve came out perfect, "solve it yourself first" seemed to recover 100% of the reference benefit at every size. Suspicious, because the numbers were exactly equal to the green curve. A code audit found a silent dispatch bug: the "solve first" arm had been running the with-reference condition twice. 128 of 128 scores identical. We retracted the finding in the log and reran everything with a verified pipeline.

The corrected experiments were more interesting than the bug:

  • Asking a 7B judge to "solve first, then judge" in one prompt makes it worse (28% vs 49%): it silently skips the solving step. Small models fail instructions quietly.
  • Forcing the two steps mechanically (generate an answer in one pass, judge with it in the next) works: that is the real purple curve, 59 / 60 / 85 / 95%.
  • Strangest of all: at 1.5B, the judge does better with its own scruffy answer as reference (59%) than with the official textbook solution (21%). Style match matters more than polish.
Six of our own results died by our own checks during this campaign. This one taught the most.
Act III · does it generalize?

Six families and a human-labeled benchmark say yes

Not a Qwen quirk, not a quirk of our planted errors.
Act IV · the real frontier

Now the hard part: domains where you cannot check the answer

Everything so far had a safety net: math has answers, code has tests. Scalable oversight is hardest precisely where that net is gone, open-ended writing, judgment calls, tasks with many valid answers. Does the reference trick, our best lever so far, still work there?

The experiment. RewardBench-2 provides graded pairs (a better and a worse response) across task types that range from fully checkable (math) to many-valid-answers questions. We ran the whole judge ladder over 460 prompts, each pair judged in both orders (if the verdict changes when you swap A and B, the judge is guessing), in three conditions: no reference, the judge's own answer as reference, and, as a control, another model's answer as reference.
Act IV · a free diagnostic

Order-swapping exposes judging without any answer key

Two things to notice. First, this measure needs no ground truth at all, you just ask twice. Second, the red line: judging precise instruction compliance ("did it really obey every constraint?") stays near chance for every judge up to 14B. That is the pairwise version of the proofreading blind spot.

Some tasks are hard for judges because they are ambiguous. Others because they require exactly the line-checking judges do not do.
Act IV · the finding

The reference lever flips sign, and we know why

The control arm settles the mechanism. If the harm came from the judge loving its own writing, other models' references would be harmless. They are not. When the judge cannot verify validity itself, any single reference anchors it on one valid answer and makes it punish other perfectly valid ones.

The dividing line: many valid answers AND verification too hard for the judge. On synthetic plural tasks whose validity is easy to check, the harm vanishes for every judge 3B and up, exactly as the model predicts.
What it all adds up to

Practical rules for anyone building oversight today

Measurement

  • Audit the grading oracle first (scorer AND key). Cheap-model consensus disagreement finds oracle bugs at 89% externally validated precision, unsupervised.
  • Never trust one threshold. Report threshold-free metrics; a cutoff manufactured a fake "7B = frontier" result.
  • Ask twice, swapped. Order-flip rate is a free, label-free stress meter for any pairwise judge.

Judges are not proofreaders

  • Explicit false steps pass 40-85% of the time; judges grade outcomes and coherence, not lines. Do not use raw judge scores as step-level process rewards.

The reference law

  1. One right answer? Provide a reference, quality matters, and even a small judge becomes reliable. No trusted reference? Have the judge generate one in a separate forced step (never "please solve first" in one prompt).
  2. Many valid answers? Withhold references entirely. Every reference, of any quality and any source, anchors the judge against valid alternatives (-7 to -8 points, p≤.0005).
  3. Precise constraint checking? No judge on our ladder can do it reliably. Use programmatic checkers, not judges.
The record

How much of this should you believe?

13findings
6own results killed by own checks
1public retraction + correction
4independent critic passes

Every headline number was re-derived from raw files with fresh code; planted code errors were re-executed against official tests; the label-noise findings rest on two frontier model families agreeing 55/55 plus a human-curated external check; the closest prior paper was audited page by page to confirm the sign-flip result is genuinely new (it tests only single-answer tasks, pointwise, no controls like ours).

Open questions we did not settle: whether verification is item-by-item bounded by generation (weak coupling, needs more data); human spot-audits of our model-based adjudications; agent-trajectory oversight (existing benchmarks cover safety labels, our planted-flaw approach there is future work); and the full frontier arms on the hard-to-verify experiments.
